use_when.01: When your team keeps correcting the same mistake instead of checking for it automatically.
use_when.02: When your product has a critical user journey that must never break silently.
use_when.03: When people or agents need to inspect changes across different worktrees or machines.
use_when.04: When you keep copying CI errors from a web page into an agent prompt.
use_when.05: When agents or newcomers keep missing project decisions, conventions or facts that are easy to overlook.
use_when.06: When your agent needs an operation that its current tools do not support.
use_when.07: When teammates or agents keep getting stuck on the same first task.
use_when.08: When agents create mismatched data shapes across storage, APIs and the user interface.
use_when.09: When a finished command leaves you unsure whether the output meets its requirements.
use_when.10: When you need to navigate unfamiliar code and handle failures from external tools safely.
use_when.11: When you add a command, route or agent operation to a codebase with a glossary and deployed API.
use_when.12: When slow, expensive work needs reusable outputs, recovery after crashes and checks for truncated artifacts.
use_when.13: When ordinary fixtures miss failures in a generator, parser, migration, transformation or widely used library.

investigations.title: Source investigations behind the handbook
investigations.h1: Follow the guides back to the source
investigations.lead: Three reports distinguish inspected code, author-reported results, remote CI records and local runs. Each separates open pull requests from merged work and links pinned source snapshots where possible. Work under an account is not necessarily written by that person.
investigations.description: Read three source investigations separating inspected code, author reports, remote CI records and local runs. Open pull requests are distinguished from merged work.
investigations._findings_comment: The findings shown on each study of investigations.html, edited from the report's own takeaway section: github-inspection.md -> 'What to take away', matt-pocock-inspection.md -> 'How this changes our guides', boris-cherny-inspection.md -> 'What this adds to the implementation package'. One sentence each, at most 22 words, beginning with a noun phrase.

github-inspection.md: A completion contract specifies the real output, how complete its inputs must be and the outcome its consumer sees.
Recurring mistakes need checks at existing lint, type, test and build boundaries that reject bad changes and accept valid ones.
Explicit ownership separates agent writes and test state, contains provider quirks in adapters and checks remote access to artifacts.
Project decisions stay beside relevant code, while evidence distinguishes local runs, remote CI, author reports and untested hardware.
matt-pocock-inspection.md: Shared vocabulary, lasting decisions, bounded modules and callable agent APIs inform the guide to speaking a codebase's language.
Output identity, resumable work and recovery from malformed results inform the guide to artifacts that survive interruptions.
The report recommends making the intended outcome easy to request and hard to misreport.
boris-cherny-inspection.md: Guide 13 adapts layered validation to test public output, reproduce new failures and preserve meaningful baselines.
Before-and-after measurements compare the same work to establish whether a change improved the result.
Existing lessons on lint, adapters and native loading provide supporting references for the skills.

ledger._comment: The closing ledger: what was run, what was not, and what is only a claim. Each row is [status, text]; status is one of RUN, LIMIT, NOT RUN, UNVERIFIED and must agree with README.md's What was checked and validation.md.
rows: The lint demo accepts the unwanted import without its rule, rejects it with the rule and accepts the supported import.
The Melee verifier passed its original nine tests and the current set of fifteen.
A synthetic comparison reproduced the completeness gap: the original verifier accepted incomplete source metrics, while the repaired version rejected them.
The verifier tests used mocked builds and establish verifier behavior only. No real game build was run.
The public applications, upload service and private agent systems were not executed for this research.
Sponsor performance claims and universal claims about careers and productivity have not been verified.
credits: Theo, Matt Pocock and Boris Cherny do not endorse this handbook.
